### Empirical Architecture Evaluation

To evaluate the resilience of this integrated harness, we measure its operational stability across an injection suite of 50 distinct physical fault profiles. Faults were categorized across four failure vectors: transport drops (SYN drops, packet loss), compute-level starvation (CPU throttling, SIGSTOP, container freezes), local storage exhaustion (`ENOSPC`, `EDQUOT`), and non-advancing model loops (syntactic retries, semantic regression).

We evaluate system survival using two primary metrics: Recovery Point Objective (RPO), defined as the count of uncommitted or untracked state mutations, and Recovery Time Objective (RTO), defined as the wall-clock interval required to resume forward execution:

$$T_{\text{RTO}} = T_{\text{detect}} + T_{\text{isolate}} + T_{\text{repair}} + T_{\text{resume}}$$

Across all 50 test scenarios, the unified harness maintained an RPO of zero uncommitted mutations ($\text{RPO} = 0$). By enforcing that every sub-transaction writes its state image and inverse compensation definition to the WAL prior to network dispatch, the storage layer never entered an indeterminate state.

| Fault Category                    | Injected Scenarios ($N$) | Mean Detection ($T_{\text{detect}}$) | Mean Recovery ($T_{\text{RTO}}$) | Primary Recovery Mechanism         | Trajectory Goodput ($G$) |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:-------------------------|
| **Transport Drop / Reset**        | 15                       | $14.2\text{ ms}$                     | $148.6\text{ ms}$                | Idempotent Transport Replay        | $0.94$                   |
| **Storage Exhaustion (`EDQUOT`)** | 10                       | $2.1\text{ ms}$                      | $182.4\text{ ms}$                | Forward Scratchpad Pruning         | $0.89$                   |
| **Worker SIGKILL / Crash**        | 10                       | $48.5\text{ ms}$                     | $1\text{,}120.0\text{ ms}$       | WAL Checkpoint Replay              | $0.78$                   |
| **Semantic Infinite Loop**        | 15                       | $4\text{,}200.0\text{ ms}$           | $6\text{,}450.0\text{ ms}$       | Watchdog Abort & Backward Rollback | $0.52$                   |

: Resilience benchmarks across 50 injected fault scenarios. Trajectory Goodput $G = \frac{\sum T_{\text{productive}}}{\sum T_{\text{total}}}$ evaluates the operational efficiency preserved by forward recovery versus backward rollback. {#tbl-synthesis-fault-metrics}

As detailed in @tbl-synthesis-fault-metrics, recovery latency varies substantially depending on whether the fault permits forward self-healing or requires backward Saga compensation. For transport drops and storage exhaustion, forward repair mechanisms resolve the failure locally, preserving high Trajectory Goodput ($G \ge 0.89$). Conversely, semantic infinite loops require watchdog timeouts ($T_{\text{detect}} \approx 4.2\text{ s}$) and full Saga compensation, depressing goodput to $0.52$.

The empirical evaluation demonstrates that relying exclusively on backward rollbacks is computationally and temporally inefficient. In distributed environments where external operations possess non-trivial latencies, the operating system must aggressively prioritize forward repair, invoking backward compensation solely when invariants are irrecoverably violated.

Having synthesized the runtime machinery required to detect, isolate, and recover from failures in autonomous execution, we now examine the common architectural fallacies and engineering pitfalls that compromise these fault-tolerant guarantees in practice.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-ch11-fallacies}

<!-- FALLACIES_SPEC:

- **Fallacy 1:** *Distributed transactions in agent systems can be governed by Two-Phase Commit (2PC).*
  - Refutation: External tools, APIs, and real-world actions lack 2PC rollback semantics; transactions must be structured as compensable Sagas.
- **Pitfall 1:** *Assuming backward rollback is always possible for mutating tools.*
  - Refutation: Many actions (sending emails, publishing packages, deleting live records) cannot be physically undone; they require semantic amendments or pivot transaction boundaries.
- **Fallacy 2:** *A running agent loop that emits heartbeats is healthy and making progress.*
  - Refutation: Agents easily enter semantic infinite loops (editing and reverting files repeatedly); progress must be measured via semantic watchdogs tracking state invariants.
- **Pitfall 2:** *Unbounded retries against a degraded external tool or database.*
  - Refutation: Generates catastrophic retry storms that crash infrastructure; runtimes must enforce circuit breakers and exponential backoff with jitter.
-->

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Distributed transactions in agent systems can be governed by Two-Phase Commit (2PC).*

Classic distributed transaction protocols such as Two-Phase Commit (2PC) presuppose a closed universe of cooperative participants that implement strict `PREPARE`, `COMMIT`, and `ABORT` primitives. In classical database engines, participants acquire exclusive read-write locks during the prepare phase, holding those locks across network boundaries until the transaction coordinator declares a global outcome. Transporting this model to agentic systems violates fundamental systems realities. First, external tools, software-as-a-service (SaaS) APIs, and operating system calls rarely expose a two-phase protocol interface; they execute side-effecting operations immediately upon invocation without providing an isolated, lockable prepare stage. Second, holding resource locks while an agent runtime samples an autoregressive model introduces catastrophic lock duration variance. Because token generation is non-deterministic and bounded by inference tail latency rather than local memory bus speeds, lock contention cascades across independent threads, causing systemic throughput collapse. If the coordinator or network fails while locks are active, resources remain locked indefinitely, violating system availability under the CAP theorem. Consequently, multi-step agent workflows cannot enforce distributed ACID isolation. They must instead adopt the Saga pattern, decomposing workflows into ordered sequences of local transactions managed by a Saga Execution Coordinator (SEC). Every step must define an explicit, compensable counter-action, substituting backward rollback and synchronous distributed locking with eventual consistency and forward-progress guarantees.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming backward rollback is always possible for mutating tools.*

Architects accustomed to relational databases often assume that failure recovery entails rewinding system state to a pristine checkpoint via backward rollback. In physical and distributed environments, however, tool actions possess directional thermodynamic entropy: once executed, physical and externally observable side effects cannot be erased. Emitting a payment via an external gateway, transmitting an email, publishing an immutable container artifact, or issuing an API request to a non-transactional downstream service irreversibly alters external state. Naively executing an inverted tool sequence under the presumption of rollback frequently creates secondary invariant violations and state drift. For instance, executing an unpublish command after external consumers have already pulled a build artifact fractures system-wide dependency graphs. Robust agent architectures must partition transactions along explicit pivot boundaries. A pivot step represents an irreversible commit point: all operations preceding the pivot must be strictly compensable, while all operations succeeding the pivot must be guaranteed to complete via forward recovery using idempotent retries and persistent queues. Furthermore, when compensation is required, systems engineers must construct semantic amendments rather than backward restorations. Depositing an offsetting ledger entry or transmitting a corrective message acknowledges that time and side effects are strictly monotonic. Attempting to restore a prior state without accounting for downstream observer mutations inevitably poisons the context window and destabilizes distributed state invariants.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A running agent loop that emits heartbeats is healthy and making progress.*

Traditional distributed systems equate operational health with liveness: as long as an operating system process responds to keep-alive pings or emits regular heartbeats, the supervisor assumes the node is functioning. In agentic runtimes, this assumption conflates transport-level liveness with algorithmic safety. Stochastic agents frequently encounter semantic livelocks, where the control loop continuously generates valid tool invocations while making zero task progress. A common failure mode is state oscillation, such as an agent alternating between modifying source code to fix a compilation error, observing a secondary lint regression, reverting its edit, and repeating the cycle indefinitely. Because token generation and API round trips continue unabated, process-level watchdogs detect continuous CPU utilization and telemetry emission, masking total execution failure. The agent accumulates tokens, exacerbating context poisoning as failed attempts clutter its context buffer, which in turn degrades the signal-to-noise ratio and reinforces the oscillatory pattern. To prevent resource starvation, execution runtimes must implement semantic watchdogs rather than transport heartbeats. A semantic watchdog tracks monotonic progress invariants over the environment state vector, such as directed acyclic graph transitions, monotonically decreasing edit distances to target specifications, or cycle detection on state hashes. If the system fails to transition across structural progress boundaries within a calibrated threshold of steps, the supervisor must preemptively abort execution and trigger compensation.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Unbounded retries against a degraded external tool or database.*

When an external tool invocation fails due to network partitions, rate limits, or transient timeouts, naive agent runtimes frequently re-invoke the failed tool in an unconstrained loop. Under degraded conditions, this policy triggers catastrophic self-amplifying feedback loops known as retry storms. When hundreds of concurrent agent loops encounter elevated tail latency or HTTP 503 Service Unavailable responses, immediate synchronous retries multiply the aggregate request volume directed at an already struggling upstream dependency. The resulting thundering herd consumes remaining database connection pools, saturates network socket queues, and exacerbates resource exhaustion, converting a localized transient fault into a cascading, system-wide outage. Furthermore, because large language model inference loops consume finite context window tokens on each logged error response, unbounded retries rapidly exhaust context allocations and dilute the task objective with repetitive stack traces. Production agent runtimes must govern external interfaces with robust resilience patterns. Invocations must pass through stateful circuit breakers that transition to an open state upon detecting error rates exceeding an operational threshold, failing fast without hitting the degraded backend. In addition, retry policies must mandate truncated exponential backoff combined with decorrelated jitter to desynchronize retry spikes across concurrent execution threads. Without these flow control barriers, autonomous retries transform transient downstream friction into permanent infrastructure collapse.

:::

<!-- FALLACIES_END -->

## Summary {#sec-vol3-ch11-summary}

Autonomous agents operating in open environments cannot rely on classical database transactions; real-world side effects executed across heterogeneous APIs, external tools, and physical systems preclude atomic isolation and instantaneous rollback. Building resilient agentic architectures requires shifting from traditional ACID guarantees to distributed Sagas and semantic compensation protocols. Within this paradigm, failure recovery is decoupled into structured forward recovery—using schema-constrained reflection, localized retry policies, and error-directed tool re-invocations—and systematic backward recovery, where an execution coordinator unwinds partially applied trajectories by issuing domain-specific inverse operations. Irreversible side effects must be isolated as explicit pivot transactions, strictly dividing compensable preliminary phases from idempotent, retriable terminal stages. Furthermore, because stochastic processors fail silently through repetitive reasoning traps, goal drift, and hallucinated task completion, fault tolerance cannot depend solely on raw process exit codes. Robust runtimes must implement semantic watchdog timers and trajectory-level progress monitors that enforce system-level invariants over state advancement. Ultimately, fault tolerance in the stochastic computer is not an emergent behavior of scale or prompt tuning, but an operating system discipline that guarantees trajectory convergence and environmental consistency in the presence of irrevocable actions.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Core Systems Principles of Fault Tolerance & Sagas"}
1. *Real-World Tools Break ACID*: Because external environments and third-party APIs lack unified two-phase commit coordinators, agent execution trajectories cannot enforce global isolation; systems must model multi-step interactions as distributed Sagas composed of observable, distinct sub-transactions.
2. *Explicit Semantic Compensation*: Every mutating sub-transaction must register a deterministic compensating action or semantic amendment capable of restoring environmental consistency when downstream tasks experience catastrophic failure.
3. *Bounded Dual-Mode Recovery*: Architectures must balance forward self-healing against backward compensation by enforcing strict, quota-bounded retry attempts before escalating to transactional unwind.
4. *Pivot Transaction Isolation*: Irrevocable mutations that permanently alter external state must be isolated as architectural pivot points, preceded entirely by compensable actions and followed strictly by retriable operations guaranteed to run to completion.
5. *Semantic Watchdog Timers*: Traditional process monitors fail to capture non-terminating cognitive loops; runtimes must implement semantic watchdogs that analyze trajectory entropy and state deltas to detect and interrupt stalled execution.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From Runtime Systems to Policy Compilers"}
With the formalization of fault tolerance, compensation protocols, and runtime lifecycle orchestration, the core architecture of the single-machine Stochastic Computer stands fully assembled: the Stochastic Processor (Chapters 2–3), the Memory Hierarchy (Chapters 4–6), Sandboxed Peripherals (Chapters 7–8), and the Operating System Runtime (Chapters 9–11). Operating this stack with off-the-shelf base models, however, exposes a critical efficiency bottleneck. Standard foundation models frequently hallucinate parameter schemas, resist backward compensation, and struggle to sustain rigorous procedural discipline across long-horizon trajectories. Compensating for these behavioral deficiencies entirely at runtime through dynamic prompting, external retries, and defensive error-trapping introduces severe latency and inference overhead. In Part V (*The Policy Compiler*), Chapter 12 (*Trajectory Data & Environmental Feedback*) begins our examination of how system designers close this loop, treating the operating system runtime as a data engine that captures operational traces, failure corrections, and execution verifications to compile runtime discipline directly into model weights.
:::
